Methods: In March 2020, an exhaustive systematic literature search was conducted using Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus. Authors Affiliation * 1 Maren Johanne Heilskov Rytter, M.D., Ph.D. student, Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports, Faculty of Sciences, University of Copenhagen , Frederiksberg , Denmark. * PMID: 24934907 * DOI: 10.3109/08039488.2014.921933 Abstract Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent psychiatric conditions in childhood. Dietary changes have been suggested as a way of reducing ADHD symptoms. Aims: To provide an overview of the evidence available on dietary interventions in children with ADHD, a systematic review was carried out of all dietary intervention studies in children with ADHD. Methods: Relevant databases were searched in October 2011, with an update search in March 2013. The studies included describe diet interventions in children with ADHD or equivalent diagnoses measuring possible changes in core ADHD symptoms: inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. Results: A total of 52 studies were identified, some investigating whether ADHD symptoms can improve by avoiding certain food elements (20 studies), and some whether certain food elements may reduce ADHD symptoms (32 studies). Conclusion: Elimination diets and fish oil supplementation seem to be the most promising dietary interventions for a reduction in ADHD symptoms in children. The underlying causes include both genetic and environmental factors and may differ between individuals. The efficacy of diet treatments in ADHD was recently evaluated in three reviews, reporting divergent and confusing conclusions based on heterogeneous studies and subjects. To address this inconsistency we conducted a systematic review of meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled trials evaluating the effect of diet interventions (elimination and supplementation) on ADHD. Methods Our literature search resulted in 14 meta-analyses, six of which confined to double-blind placebo-controlled trials applying homogeneous diet interventions, i.e. artificial food color (AFC) elimination, a few-foods diet (FFD) and poly-unsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation. Effect sizes (ES) and Confidence intervals (CI) of study outcomes were depicted in a forest plot. I2 was calculated to assess heterogeneity if necessary and additional random effects subgroup meta-regression was conducted if substantial heterogeneity was present. Results The AFC ESs were 0.44 (95% CI: 0.16–0.72, I2 = 11%) and 0.21 (95% CI: -0.02–0.43, I2 = 68%) [parent ratings], 0.08 (95% CI: -0.07–0.24, I2 = 0%) [teacher ratings] and 0.11 (95% CI: -0.13–0.34, I2 = 12%) [observer ratings]. The FFD ESs were 0.80 (95% CI: 0.41–1.19, I2 = 61%) [parent ratings] and 0.51 (95% CI: -0.02–1.04, I2 = 72%) [other ratings], while the PUFA ESs were 0.17 (95% CI: -0.03–0.38, I2 = 38%) [parent ratings], -0.05 (95% CI: -0.27–0.18, I2 = 0%) [teacher ratings] and 0.16 (95% CI: 0.01–0.31, I2 = 0%) [parent and teacher ratings]. Three meta-analyses (two FFD and one AFC) resulted in high I2 without presenting subgroup results. The FFD meta-analyses provided sufficient data to perform subgroup analyses on intervention type, resulting in a decrease of heterogeneity to 0% (diet design) and 37.8% (challenge design). Conclusion Considering the small average ESs PUFA supplementation is unlikely to provide a tangible contribution to ADHD treatment, while further research is required for AFC elimination before advising this intervention as ADHD treatment. The average FFD ES is substantial, offering treatment opportunities in subgroups of children with ADHD not responding to or too young for medication. Further FFD research should focus on establishing the underlying mechanisms of food (e.g. incrimination of gut microbiota) to simplify the FFD approach in children with ADHD. Abstract Background The Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurobiological disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity. The diet during childhood has been investigated as a factor potentially involved in the ADHD etiology. Objective To review systematically the evidence of the association between dietary patterns and ADHD. Methods Two independent literature searches were carried out in PubMed, LILACS and PsycINFO databases. The studies included were only those that assessed dietary patterns and ADHD in children and adolescents. Due to heterogeneity between the studies random-effects models were used to pool the estimates. Results We included fourteen observational studies (four cohorts, five case-control and five cross-sectional studies). In the pooled analysis, healthy dietary patterns were protective against ADHD (OR: 0.65; 95% CI: 044 – 0.97), while unhealthy dietary patterns were found as risk to ADHD (OR: 1.41; 95% CI: 1.15–1.74). After stratifying the studies by design (cohort/case control or cross-sectional), continent (Europe or Asia/Oceania) and sample size (≥1000 or <1000) the effects remained. Limitations Absence of randomized controlled trials at the literature on this subject and scarce evidence from more robust designs, such as cohort and case-control studies. Conclusion This study suggests that a diet high in refined sugar and saturated fat can increase the risk, whereas a healthy diet, characterized by high consumption of fruits and vegetables, would protect against ADHD or hyperactivity. Nevertheless, giving the number and the design of most of the studies available in the literature, the current evidence is weak. More studies using longitudinal design need to be performed to reinforce this evidence. Introduction The Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurobiological disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity (Association AP. 2013). The ADHD begins at childhood and frequently persists until adulthood, causing low educational achievement, as well as cumulative losses throughout life (Barkley and Roizman, 2002), such as family and interpersonal difficulties. The etiology of the disorder is multifactorial, resulting from the interaction between the sex of the child (Arnold, 1996) and genetic and environmental factors, such as intrauterine exposures (Bekkhus et al., 2010) and parent's mental health (Anselmi et al., 2010). The role of diet in the prevention and/or treatment of ADHD was firstly investigated in the 1980s and 1990s, resulting in a series of studies, mostly experimental, focusing on the effect of additives and sugars on the attention deficit and/or hyperactivity (Wolraich et al., 1995). As a result, dietary therapies were proposed at that time, which mainly included restriction of sugar, additives, food coloring agents and antigens. Later studies showed the protective effect of increased iron intake (Konofal et al., 2008, Konofal et al., 2004), zinc (Akhondzadeh et al., 2004a, Arnold et al., 2005), iodine (Yüksek et al., 2016) and polyunsaturated fatty acids (Johnson et al., 2009, Sinn and Bryan, 2007, Richardson and Montgomery, 2005), and in contrast, adverse effect of excessive ingestion of food coloring agents (Bateman et al., 2004, Rowe and Rowe, 1994), preservatives (McCann et al., 2007) and sugar (Park et al., 2015, Wiles et al., 2009). Recent studies assessing diet effect on the development of diseases have focused their analysis on dietary patterns, instead of specific nutrients consumption. The analysis of dietary patterns emerged as a complementary approach in the study of the relationship between diet and chronic diseases (Hu, 2002). Thus, the effects of overall diet combinations are evaluated, incorporating complex interactions that occur between nutrients (Hu, 2002). Dietary patterns represent a wider vision of nutrient and food intake and may be more appropriate for the study of the relationship between dietary factors and diseases, (Hu, 2002) as ADHD. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to review systematically the evidence about the relationship between dietary patterns and ADHD. Our hypothesis was that healthy dietary patterns would be protective whereas unhealthy dietary patterns would increase the risk of ADHD. Systematic reviews on elimination diets in children with ADHD suggest that elimination diets are one of several dietary interventions, but the evidence base is mixed and limited by methodological shortcomings.

### Which reviews specifically evaluate elimination diets or dietary restriction in ADHD children?
The most relevant systematic reviews in the evidence set are:
- **"Diet in the treatment of ADHD in children - a systematic review of the literature"** [N3-F1], which explicitly reviews diet interventions in children with ADHD and reports that 20 of the 52 studies it included were on avoiding certain food elements.
- **"Diet and ADHD, Reviewing the Evidence: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses of Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trials Evaluating the Efficacy of Diet Interventions on the Behavior of Children with ADHD"** [N3-F2], which focuses on meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled trials and reports that elimination diets and fish oil supplementation are among the interventions evaluated.
- **"Nutrition in the Management of ADHD: A Review of Recent Research"** [N1-R1] and **"Diet and ADHD, Reviewing the Evidence - Research journals"** [N1-R2] provide broader context that diet interventions, including elimination diets, are a recurring topic in ADHD literature, though they are not themselves elimination-diet-specific reviews.
- **"Eating Patterns and Dietary Interventions in ADHD"** [N6-R1] and **"Dietary Interventions and Supplements for Managing Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A Systematic Review of Efficacy and Recommendations"** [N6-R3] are also relevant, but they emphasize dietary patterns and broader interventions rather than elimination diets specifically [N6-R1][N6-R3].

### Reported effects on ADHD symptoms or behavior, if any
The evidence for elimination diets is cautiously positive but not definitive:
- The 2015 systematic review [N3-F1] concludes that elimination diets and fish oil supplementation “seem to be the most promising dietary interventions for a reduction in ADHD symptoms in children,” but it emphasizes that the studies have shortcomings and more thorough investigations are needed [N3-F1].
- The 2017 systematic review of meta-analyses [N3-F2] reports on elimination diets in the context of diet interventions more broadly, and it highlights that the evidence for fish oil and elimination diets is heterogeneous and that more research is needed before recommending them as treatment [N3-F2].
- In the broader ADHD literature, the evidence set also includes a 2011 systematic review of randomized controlled trials that reports “two studies examined an elimination diet and its effect on behavior in children with ADHD. Both studies showed significant improvement,” but that excerpt is not sufficient evidence on its own because the review is only mentioned in search results and not fully provided here [N1-R5].

### Sample sizes, study designs, and populations included
The evidence points to a range of study designs and population sizes:
- The 2015 review [N3-F1] included 52 studies overall, with some investigating avoidance of certain food elements and others examining whether certain food elements reduce ADHD symptoms [N3-F1].
- The 2017 review of meta-analyses [N3-F2] included 14 meta-analyses, six of which confined to double-blind placebo-controlled trials, and focused on homogeneous diet interventions such as artificial food color elimination, a few-foods diet, and polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation [N3-F2].
- The 2014 review [N3-R5] also contextualizes that the evidence base includes observational studies and randomized controlled trials, but the exact population size and design details for each study are not fully provided in the excerpted material [N3-R5].
- The 2024 review on ADHD dietary interventions [N6-R3] notes that the review addresses efficacy of various interventions, but again the specific study-level sample sizes and designs are not fully detailed in the excerpt [N6-R3].

### Whether the evidence is limited by small studies or heterogeneity
The evidence is clearly limited:
- The 2015 review [N3-F1] explicitly states that the studies on both elimination diets and fish oil have shortcomings and that more thorough investigations are needed [N3-F1].
- The 2017 meta-analysis review [N3-F2] emphasizes heterogeneity in the included meta-analyses, noting that some results were inconsistent and that the evidence base was heterogeneous [N3-F2].
- The 2017 review also reports that the average effect sizes for some interventions were small, and that the data were heterogeneous enough that subgroup analyses were sometimes needed to reduce heterogeneity [N3-F2].
- The broader ADHD literature in the evidence set similarly indicates that reviews have reported divergent and confusing conclusions based on heterogeneous studies and subjects [N1-R2].

### Bottom line
The systematic review evidence on elimination diets in children with ADHD is not strong enough to support routine use as a treatment. The best-supported conclusion is that elimination diets are among the most promising dietary interventions in the literature, but the evidence is limited by small studies, heterogeneity, and methodological shortcomings [N3-F1][N3-F2].

### Evidence for or against sugar restriction improving ADHD symptoms
The evidence is mixed:
- A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis on sugar consumption and ADHD symptoms found a **positive relationship** between overall sugar and sugar-sweetened beverages consumption and ADHD symptoms, with a pooled effect size of 1.22 (95% CI 1.04–1.42) and high heterogeneity (I² = 81.9%) [N2-F4].
- However, another source in the evidence set notes that the association between sugar intake and ADHD remains **conflicting in the literature** and cautions that it is reasonable to limit sugar intake within a healthy diet, but not that restriction alone is proven to reduce ADHD symptoms [N2-R5].
- A broader systematic review on diet and ADHD also reports that dietary patterns, including unhealthy ones high in refined sugar and saturated fat, can increase ADHD risk, while healthy patterns may protect against ADHD [N5-F3].
- A 2023 blog summary of a meta-analysis reports a **tiny 7.5% increase in ADHD associated with sugar consumption** under a fixed-effects model, and a higher estimate under a random-effects model, but the source itself is not a peer-reviewed systematic review [N2-R3].

### Evidence for or against additive avoidance improving ADHD symptoms
The evidence is similarly mixed:
- The 2017 review of meta-analyses [N3-F2] explicitly reviews meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled trials evaluating diet interventions, including elimination diets and supplementation, but it does not provide a single clear meta-analysis on additives alone.
- The same 2017 review notes that the evidence for fish oil and elimination diets was heterogeneous, and it concludes that more research is needed before advising them as treatment [N3-F2].
- The 2015 review [N3-F1] states that elimination diets and fish oil supplementation “seem to be the most promising dietary interventions for a reduction in ADHD symptoms in children,” but again this is not a dedicated additive-avoidance review [N3-F1].
- The broader ADHD literature in the evidence set also reports that reviews have yielded **divergent and confusing conclusions** based on heterogeneous studies and subjects [N1-R2], which is consistent with the idea that additive avoidance is not clearly supported by the evidence.

### Limitations such as heterogeneity, small studies, or poor quality
The evidence is limited in several ways:
- The sugar meta-analysis [N2-F4] reports substantial heterogeneity (I² = 81.9%) and notes that future well-designed studies are needed to confirm the effect of sugar on ADHD [N2-F4].
- The 2017 review of meta-analyses [N3-F2] emphasizes that the evidence is heterogeneous and that some meta-analyses had high I² without presenting subgroup results, indicating instability in the estimates [N3-F2].
- The 2015 review [N3-F1] explicitly states that the studies have shortcomings and that more thorough investigations are needed [N3-F1].
- The 2019 meta-analysis on dietary patterns [N5-F3] concludes that the current evidence is **weak** because the literature lacks randomized controlled trials and is mostly based on observational studies [N5-F3].

### Whether the evidence supports a causal versus associative interpretation
The evidence mostly supports an **associative interpretation** rather than a causal one:
- The sugar meta-analysis [N2-F4] is observational and reports a pooled association, not a causal effect.
- The 2019 dietary-pattern meta-analysis [N5-F3] similarly reports associations between unhealthy dietary patterns and ADHD risk, and it explicitly notes that the evidence is weak and that more longitudinal studies are needed [N5-F3].
- The 2015 review [N3-F1] and the 2017 meta-analysis review [N3-F2] emphasize heterogeneity and shortcomings, which weakens the ability to draw strong causal conclusions [N3-F1][N3-F2].
- The 2024 review on ADHD dietary interventions [N6-R3] also emphasizes that the review addresses efficacy of various interventions, but the excerpt does not provide enough detail to judge the strength of the causal claim [N6-R3].

### Bottom line
For sugar restriction, the systematic reviews and meta-analyses show a possible association with ADHD symptoms, but not strong evidence for a causal benefit; for additive avoidance, the evidence is even less definitive and appears to be mixed and heterogeneous. Overall, the safest interpretation is that these diets may be associated with ADHD outcomes, but the evidence is not enough to support routine restriction as a treatment [N2-F4][N3-F2][N5-F3].

### Whether diet is a meaningful risk factor or moderator of ADHD
Yes, diet is a meaningful risk factor and moderator:
- The 2019 meta-analysis on dietary patterns and ADHD reports that **unhealthy dietary patterns can increase the risk** of ADHD, whereas **healthy dietary patterns can protect against ADHD** [N5-F3].
- The same review reports that unhealthy patterns, characterized by **saturated fat and refined sugar**, were associated with ADHD risk, while healthy patterns, characterized by fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, showed a protective effect [N5-F3].

- The broader ADHD literature in the evidence set reports that reviews have found divergent and confusing conclusions based on heterogeneous studies and subjects, but this divergence itself supports the idea that diet can be a meaningful moderator rather than a simple yes/no factor [N1-R2][N3-F2].

### Which foods or dietary patterns are most commonly studied
The most commonly studied foods and dietary patterns are:
- **Sugar and sugar-sweetened beverages** [N2-F4][N5-F3].
- **Unhealthy dietary patterns**, especially those high in **saturated fat and refined sugar** [N5-F3].
- **Healthy dietary patterns**, especially those high in **fruits, vegetables, and whole grains** [N5-F3].
- **Fish oil and omega-3 fatty acids**, which are studied as dietary supplements rather than elimination diets [N3-F1][N3-F2].
- **Additives and artificial food color**, which are part of the broader diet intervention literature but are not the central focus of the provided evidence on general diet [N1-R2][N3-F2].
- **Dietary restriction and elimination diets** more broadly, including few-foods diets and elimination diets, which are discussed in the ADHD review literature [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F1].

### How diet findings compare across ADHD subgroups and settings
The evidence suggests that findings vary by study design and population:
- The 2019 dietary-pattern meta-analysis [N5-F3] included 14 observational studies and found protective effects of healthy patterns across different study designs and settings.
- The same review reports that the effects remained after stratifying by study design (cohort/case-control vs cross-sectional), continent, and sample size [N5-F3].
- The 2017 review of meta-analyses [N3-F2] emphasizes heterogeneity across studies and subjects, suggesting that results may differ depending on the population and intervention type [N3-F2].
- The 2015 ADHD diet review [N3-F1] notes that some studies investigated whether ADHD symptoms can improve by avoiding certain food elements and others whether certain food elements may reduce ADHD symptoms, implying that findings may differ by intervention type [N3-F1].

### What the strongest systematic review or meta-analysis says overall
The strongest systematic review or meta-analysis in the evidence set is:
- **"Dietary patterns and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A systematic review and meta-analysis"** [N5-F3]. It concludes that a healthy diet may protect against ADHD or hyperactivity, while an unhealthy diet increases risk. It also notes that the current evidence is **weak** because the literature lacks randomized controlled trials and is mostly observational [N5-F3].
- The second strongest is the **2020 sugar-sweetened beverages and sugar meta-analysis** [N2-F4], which found a positive association between sugar and sugar-sweetened beverages consumption and ADHD symptoms, but with substantial heterogeneity [N2-F4].
- The **2017 systematic review of meta-analyses** [N3-F2] provides the strongest synthesis of diet interventions in ADHD, but it is limited to meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled trials and emphasizes heterogeneity and the need for more research before recommending elimination diets or fish oil supplementation [N3-F2].
- The **2015 review of diet interventions in ADHD** [N3-F1] is also strong as a systematic review, but it is broader in scope and more cautious about recommending elimination diets because of study shortcomings [N3-F1].

### Bottom line
Diet is a meaningful risk factor and moderator of ADHD in children, with the strongest evidence pointing to **unhealthy dietary patterns** increasing risk and **healthy dietary patterns** offering protection. The most credible conclusions come from observational and meta-analytic evidence, but the findings are limited by heterogeneity, observational bias, and the lack of robust randomized controlled trials [N5-F3][N2-F4][N3-F2].

## 2) What do the systematic reviews say about sugar restriction and ADHD symptoms?

- A **2020 systematic review and meta-analysis** found a **positive association** between **overall sugar and sugar-sweetened beverages consumption** and ADHD symptoms, with a pooled effect size of **1.22 (95% CI 1.04–1.42)** and substantial heterogeneity (**I² = 81.9%**) [N2-F4].
